description: Learn what this workshop covers and how it will help you build a local AI workflow that fits your own hardware and use cases.
Install LM Studio and run a small local model so you have a working setup before we explore the details.
Learn when local models make sense, where cloud frontier models are stronger, and why local AI skills matter to companies.
Learn what a model is, how neural networks use weights and parameters, and why open weights are just files full of numbers.
See how language becomes tokens, how an LLM predicts text one token at a time, and how context and sampling settings affect its output.
Learn how CPUs, GPUs, RAM, VRAM, and unified memory affect whether a local model fits and how quickly it can generate text.
Learn how to read a model name and what model families are.
Learn how to search Hugging Face, evaluate a model repository, and identify the right files to download.
Learn the common types of AI models and how to choose one that matches the task you want to perform.
Learn what dense models, mixture-of-experts models, and multi-token prediction mean for local model performance.
Learn why model files need a compatible runtime and how formats such as GGUF and MLX affect a local setup.
Learn which hardware details affect local models and how we will use them to find compatible models on Hugging Face.
See how quantization reduces model memory use, why names such as Q4 and Q8 matter, and how to choose a first download.
Estimate a model's memory needs before downloading it, then verify the estimate with a controlled load test.
Learn how to read a model card for the prompt template, chat template, and generation settings a local model expects.
Learn which local-model performance metrics matter and how to compare models without changing every variable at once.
Learn how LM Studio turns a loaded local model into an OpenAI-compatible API that developer tools can use.
Learn the shared configuration pattern for connecting an editor, CLI, or coding agent to LM Studio.
Connect VS Code to LM Studio in both Agent mode and regular chat mode.
Configure Pi to use LM Studio models.
Learn when remote access makes sense and choose between LM Link and a manual Tailscale connection without exposing your model server publicly.
Use LM Link to make a model loaded on another computer available through your local LM Studio server.
Connect a client to an LM Studio server over a private Tailscale network.
Rent a more powerful machine to run your own local model server when buying new hardware does not make sense yet.
